I'm thinking it may be worth taking the parameterisation / class finding out of the component implementation for now. If we are targetting these objects to be passive in the future then adding in the parameters etc. adds complexity that will likely then have to be removed. We can always add it back in later if we decide components need to know about their parameterisation or to be further subclassed.

We've discussed this a bit further - `Component` will be a passive data structure in bluemira, so what we really want to reflect the `ReactorSystem` equivalent is a kind of `Builder` class that encodes the logic to create/design the components and a `ComponentManager` to handle the built components. That should give a better separated class structure.

In the shorter term we can use `Component` to build the tree(s) in parallel with the BLUEPRINT functionality.

@CoronelBuendia made a fair point offline that the idea to keep `Component` as a minimal class means that this module will not be so likely to grow, so it's probably worth moving it to the `base` module.

maybe we could also agree on how to structure relative imports, and what to expose at the module `__init__.py` level. I have a nasty habit or never using relative imports and almost never exposing things in `__init__.py` ...

Relative imports would mean that the 'running the file runs the corresponding test' wouldn't work... I think (relative imports only work for modules and not scripts). I would probably prefer using relative imports over the script invoking the tests, but worth being clear about that implied change.

Exposing the right (public) stuff in `__init__.py`, and appropriate use of `__all__` is worth going over a the same time, yes

Agreed, I think this can just go ahead as proposed.

The methods have been proposed only for the _shape part but, using the same dictionary strategy, it should be almost easy to extend it to a BluemiraGeo instance (added in the additional context). For the moment I am only going to define the serialize/deserialize as class methods (e.g. BluemiraGeo.serialize()) that return/"eat" a simple dict. Not going to implement a json interface. That should be common to all the serializable object... out of the scope of this proposal. Is it fine for you, @DanShort12 ?

Ah, this one was actually intentional; it's hopefully a historical issue now though. For EU-DEMO the TF WP cross-section was defined in a slightly different way to how PROCESS (around 2015) handled it. The ground insulation (at the time 8 mm) was to be wrapped around the winding pack. The winding pack was then to be inserted (during manufacture) inside the steel casing (which comes in several parts). The plasma-facing "front" casing was then to be welded onto the rest of the casing (again in multiple parts), thus enclosing the winding pack in the steel structure. Due to inevitable manufacturing tolerances of such large components, it was deemed necessary to include what was called an insertion gap (10 mm at the time). The resulting void was to be filled by introducing a liquid resin which would later be cured. It was felt that the insertion gap on the inboard was going to be predominantly to one side in the radial direction. I'm fairly sure that the WP was to be more or less flush to the inboard casing (including the ground insulation) and that the insertion gap was to lie on the outer edge of the inboard winding pack.

PROCESS at the time instead put the insertion gap on all sides of the winding pack, instead of just one. This may have been fixed now. @sebkahn and @jmorris-uk might know more.

OK, so after extensive brainstorming today with Mark - the plan for this is currently as follows:

Initially: write a new Optimiser(EquilibriumOptimiser) as suggested by Matti, that minimises the objective function $` \mathcal L `$ (by passing to NLOpt or similar) that includes the divertor figure of merit. The choice of the objective function is broad, and should ideally be guided by the actual requirements imposed by the physics at the divertor, as mentioned by Matti - possibly being user-defined. In lieu of this, the initial objective function as a function of coil currents to minimise will be

```math
\mathcal L ({\bf I}) = \lambda_1 \left(||\bf{GI} -\bf{b_t} + \bf{b_p}||^2_2 +||\bf{\Gamma I}||^2_2\right) - \lambda_2 L_c({\bf I}) - \lambda_3 f_x({\bf I})
```

with the $`\lambda_i >0`$ for $`i= 1,2,3`$ that weight the relative importance of the magnetic constraints (containing the four main isoflux constraints the constrain the core), the connection length, and the flux expansion to be specified by the user. The previous set of constraints on I, B etc will be applied as before, with the extra x-point constraint supplemented to this as required. This also makes it straightforward to check consistency with the existing coil current optimisation procedure, by setting $`\lambda_2 = \lambda_3 = 0`$.

This route should be able to be extended in a rather straightforward manner if coil positions need to be optimised in the same step, and to accommodate different/better objective functions as the divertor optimisation problem becomes better defined.

If the magnetic constraints are more or less well-met, then solutions with very different coil positions can be equivalent in the magnetostatic sense. There are control problems associated with very whacky coil positions that might still solve the static problem, but generally for a reasonable number of coils I think it will be OK. We run an EquilibriumConverger on the resulting coilsets (with all the optimised coil positions) and if this fails then it's a failed run.

Honestly, without profiling that problem properly, I shouldn't have said anything as to where I thought the bottlenecks are. We calculate the response matrices every time, and for the force and field constraints, we care about values inside the coils, and resort to the semi-analytic calculations which are much slower than `greens_..`. The Jacobians of the constraints and obj function are calculated analytically.

We do separate position and current optimisation steps, the latter nested in the former so it looks something like:
* get a reasonable starting point (equilibrium)
* optimise coil positions
  * for given coil positions, optimise coil currents
* converge equilibrim(a) for given coilset

There are a lot of ways that this could be sped up. And I'm open to all of them! Profiling should come first though. Things will likely depend on the number of magnetic constraints being used, and the number of coils. Food for thought.

    def offset_pyclipper(self, delta):

        loop offset using the pycliper methods
        """
        # Making the coordinates a list if (x,z) points
        loop_coordinates = np.array([self.x, self.z])
        loop_coordinates = loop_coordinates.T

        # Defining the clipper offset object
        clipper_offset = pyclipper.PyclipperOffset()

        # Calculate the scale value to be put in pyclipper
        coordinates_scaled = pyclipper.scale_to_clipper(loop_coordinates)

the possibility to use gmsh (+ different gmsh python api) as only geometry and mesh tool was taken into account ~2 years ago during the definition of the architecture of mirapy (one of the code "merged" into bluemira). In our group there was already a certain knowledge of gmsh and, indeed, it would have been our preferred option.

However, after some tests, that approach was considered not appropriate for our application considering both performances and project time schedule. In short, the need to have a robust object-oriented interface with gmsh would have brought us to write a lot of code that was already implemented and tested into FreeCAD (I usually don't like to "reinvent the wheel" :) ). Moreover, it looks to me that the efficiency of very simple operations (like calculation of lengths, areas, and volumes, highly used in optimization procedures) using only gmsh would have been very poor since a pre-mesh process is needed. Also manipulation of parametric curves doesn't seem so "easy".

My personal opinion is that gmsh is a good tool for a "static" generation of geometry and mesh (indeed it has been chosen as core-tool for the meshing module), while it doesn't offer the needed flexibility in a "dynamic" approach. Btw, if you have another option (maybe based on a better knowledge of gmsh than mine), I am more than happy to have a discussion with you and check other alternatives.

Well the reference point was fundamentally, the production of robust meshable CAD is actually quite difficult, the primary issues (with regards to downstream physics applications) is the shared topology between volumes (surfaces), this of course can be backed out once one has a STEP file (sometimes) it would be better (best?) to have that shared topology inherent in the creation of the objects. This is something that gmsh fundamentally allows, and furthermore using the OCC part of gmsh, would allow for that geometry to be (1) inherently meshable with the appropriate metadata defined as curve/surface boundary conditions and surface/volume blocks/regions. In my experience, actually metadata is the roughest part, especially BC's. We can mesh BLUEPRINT CAD right now, however, it means loosing (whatever) metadata is currently present. If we hope to automate FEA in the future, which I presume you would, this would nessessitate a close integration of GMSH, frankly to the point of it actually being the geometry kernel. 

Further, 1) this tight integration and 2) shared topology, actually fights against the concepts of object orientation, since one can no longer talk of a 'vv' object without referencing the 'blanket' since there will be shared topology between them, but this is necessary since it removes the possibility of overlaps (due to reusing the topology and hence it being shared). It is of course possible, to ask for a STEP instantiation of this geometry from GMSH, which looses all the shared topology, but when you want to build it back it is trivially possible (BREP). 

With regards to the specific point 'Moreover, it looks to me that the efficiency of very simple operations (like calculation of lengths, areas, and volumes, highly used in optimization procedures) using only gmsh would have been very poor since a pre-mesh process is needed. Also manipulation of parametric curves doesn't seem so "easy" ', I dont know, I presume when constructing objects through the OCC interface of GMSH one can ask for the area as you would with FreeCAD or PyOCC, if not I'm sure it could be added seeing is the OCC interface is a very thing wrapper around OCC itself. With regards to manipulation, what do you plan on doing?

I say all this knowing that meshing is the final stage of the CAD process 'lets not have the tail wag the dog', but actually it would be easy to paint yourself into an 'un-meshable' corner by ignoring. I also know that it fights against the OO nature of what you're trying to do. I also say this with being familiar with geometry creation in a range of libraries/settings. One final thought, https://cadquery.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ is an up and coming CAD library (OCC of course) and even worse, relies upon CONDA, anyone who knows me will know how I must be saying this through gritted teeth. However, it can produce directly meshable BREP files, which cannot be produced easily via FreeCAD. 

Thats my two cents....

Here is how I coped with this problem in MIRA. Anywhere in the core classes (solvers, geometry builder, etc.), the SI units are used, meaning that any class properties or input parameters to each method are implicitly meant to feature and operate with SI units. 
However, there are few exceptions to evaluate case by case, such as:
* plasma density [1E19/m^3] or also [1E20/m^3]. On that, I believe it's all about making a choice based on practical convenience, and that will apply to all plasma physics-related modules, such as SOL physics or particle heat fluxes calculation. So the normal "Praxis" would suggest using [1E19/m^3], I guess. Another option would be to assume pure atomic concentrations, i.e. particles/m^3 or mol/m^3. That would fulfil the SI criterion and be more coherent.
* plasma ion and electron temperature [keV]. Again, here is another purely plasma-physics related unit, meaning that one will handle these variables only in certain plasma physics solvers. However, I assume we will rely on external MHD solvers, meaning that these will eventually dictate the units of the parameters they take as inputs (e.g. PLASMOD reads the temperature at the plasma separatrix in keV). It would be rather tedious to continuously convert a plasma temperature from K to keV and from keV to K, also because plasma temperatures in K would yield non-comprehensive scales. So, in this case, I would simply make a choice based on the application (and the much larger convenience of using keV rather than using K). Actually, it all comes down to the kinetic energy of plasma particles than purely temperature-related values.
* neutron flux density [n/cm^2/s] or [n/m^2/s]. In MIRA I decided to be consistent with the full SI unit rules, i.e. using n/m^2/s. The radiation transport codes operate with cm for the XS and with n/cm^2/s for the flux densities. And that is something to keep in mind when doing I/O parsing operations to and from these codes (I assume that holds for OpenMC. too). This is a problem that we encounter when running external solvers within bluemira, and that is also the case for the physics unit listed above when running PLASMOD.

Finally, from the user side, I use ad-hoc methods or multiplications constants, to perform units conversion. But that occurs from the user-interface (or main) script, i.e. the one that runs the full configurations.

> A general philosophy comment. Is it better to create an N-arc class rather than a specific number of arcs? That may be too much for right now but it seem's silly to do it for specific numbers of arcs.

Definitely crossed my mind! Obviously there is an infinite set of N-tuple arcs, and 2 times infinity for the symmetric and asymmetric cases. Problems:
* Making `n_arcs` a variable would make the optimisation of such a parameterisation a mixed-integer problem. This would drastically reduce the number of optimisers capable of handling it. NLopt, for example, does not support mixed-integer problems.
* You could dynamically generate classes for a reasonable range of `n_arc`s, but I feel these would be a bit difficult to test and document.
* If you tend towards `n_arcs` being very large, you probably just want to use splines.

Right now, we're also missing a pretty important thing on `GeometryParameterisations`, namely some variable consistency constraint equations. For example, you could specify a set of variable values that produce a nonsense shape, such as all radii being 0, or all angles being 360. Before taking these further, I need to add in some constraints for that kind of stuff. Then we might see just how flexible an `NArc` would be.

I've addressed the majority of the comments as discussed with @ivanmaione.

I still have concerns that we are trying to abstract out matplotlib a little too much here. If users want super-customised plots, to some extent they are free to go and make whatever plot they want (using whatever library): the data is there. We should only offer some default plots, and some ways of changing them slightly. If they want to add titles or colorbars or whatever, the matplotlib `Axes` are there for that.

There are two outstanding issues that I can see:
* It is way too complicated to modify the plotting options. This is demonstrated by the fact that in the previous version of the tutorial, the default plotting options were being set my modifying (!) a global constant in a private module. It should be possible to do something like:
  ```python 
  plot_2d(something, ax=ax, **my_options)
  ```
  or at the very least
  ```python
  plot_2d(something, ax=ax, options=Plot2DOptions(**my_options))
  ```
  at present this is not possible, and the only way to change the behaviour in the (I stress) _only_ user-facing plotting functions `plot_2d` `plot_3d` `show_cad` and `component.*` is to import a private class from a private module and use that, modify the global constants (!) or write a subclass from `DisplayOptions` that magically implements all of the keys in the private `DEFAULT` dictionary(s). There must be a better way. I didn't dare modify this, as it seems there is a sort of `ABC` structure in place, and I didn't want to break anything that was intended to be built around this architecture... Suffice to say we need to be able to easily change the appearance of plots. 
* Matplotlib's `show` and `block` behave very differently in a Python terminal than in an IPython terminal or Jupyter notebook (see https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.show.html). I believe we are doing too much to insulate the user from matplotlib here. It is a standard Python library, and some literacy in it is a prerequisite. Here, we are taking on too much "baggage" trying to set `show` and `block` everywhere. In my view, it should be up to the user to configure their IDE "correctly" such that plots are shown, or simply to call `plt.show()` or `plt.ion()` in a terminal, if that is what they want to do. We cannot afford to second-guess everybody's IDE + configuration set-up.

1. Available plot options
I think what we have now is fine, and hopefully won't require much extension as we develop stuff. Having separate points, wire, and face options is OK for me, as it gives a lot of flexibility. I guess I meant performing various activities on the matplotlib `Figure` and `Axes` should not be done in the `Plotter` classes, as the users should just use matplotlib. The figure and ax are always "accessible" more or less directly.

2. and 3. Modifiying plot options
You're right, things are better already! Nevertheless, even for let's say "developer" use, using the various `PointsPlotter`, `FacePlotter`, etc. I think it should be really easy to modify the behaviour by directly passing some options in. This is now possible.

In this example:
```python
my_group_options = FacePlotter().options.as_dict()
my_group_options["wire_options"] = {}
my_group_options["face_options"] = {"color": "red"}
group = GroupingComponent("Components")
c1 = PhysicalComponent("Comp1", face, parent=group)
c2 = PhysicalComponent("Comp2", wface, parent=group)
c3 = PhysicalComponent("Comp3", w1face, parent=group)
group.plot_2d(**my_group_options)
```
Note that we import a sort of "developer" plotter, extract the underlying `DisplayOptions` subclass (in this case for `BluemiraFace`s) as a dictionary, and pass into a `ComponentPlotter` (which in this case has faces). A lot of my comments centre around the way things are done in the plotting tutorial, which is perhaps not fair because at the moment it is sort of like a development and testing playground. Like the above for instance, feels convoluted, but as you say (which I hadn't noticed) it is also possible to access component plot options via `plot_*_options`, so one can in fact now directly do:

```python
my_group_options = {"wire_options": {}, "face_options": {"color": "red"}, "show_points": False}
group.plot_2d(**my_group_options)
```

or if one isn't sure what options are available, just `print(group.plot_2d_options.as_dict())`. I think we should expose the most simple and also recommended use in the tutorial.

So, in summary, we are now really getting there, and I think most of my comments are addressed already. I will put in a couple more modifications to the tutorial, just to perfect my understanding of the functionality, and make sure that it shows the "simplest" way of doing things. After cleaning up the sections of the split up first wall, they no longer formally intersected, resulting in a weird kink that  caused the inner and outer profiles to intersect (and so Geometry Error was raised with the shell was created). Changing the order of logic - finding the outer profile as the union of shapes _before_ subtracting the inner profile to get the wall shapes fixed this. In addition, I removed the check in the first wall test that the divertor section intersects with the  inboard and outboard pieces, because they no longer do (formally, if you zoom in to 10^-4 you can resolve the gap). There isn't any logic which depends on this condition holding, so I felt it was OK to remove it.

Another fix added, this time on the divertor cassette recipe. Turns out that subtracting the divertor wall from the cassette no longer worked properly after cleaning the divertor loop as it was now ~10^-4 away from the bottom of the cassette box loop, so the inner and outer pieces were joined by a sliver. Subtracting the full outer profile fixes this.

My two cents: the heat flux model as it stands is only valid for first wall heat fluxes from charged particles. It does not include radiation in the SOL, or charge exchange effects. The fact that a DN is never really a DN is, I think, always true: the distance between the primary and secondary separatrices at the outboard midplane can be very small, but I don't think it can actually physically be 0. This proposal would change how we treat the charged particles from the primary to the secondary separatrix, because the power would only go to the primary targets. In practice, equilibria solved with symmetry will probably have a dr_sep|OMP roughly around machine or interpolation precision. DN equilibria solved without symmetry would have a more realistic dr_sep|OMP, but usually shouldn't be large. Either way, I doubt this would change the power on the first wall very much, because we're only talking about a few flux surfaces very close to the primary separatrix which should not intersect the first wall (with a reasonable FW design).

We know that this model is not "valid" for divertor heat fluxes, and I think this proposal will mostly affect these. Changing the way the power to the divertor is spread for a few flux surfaces shouldn't change the heat fluxes on the first wall very much. It will, slightly, because of the power integral corrections, but this should be minor.

Much more sophisticated models (e.g. SOLPS) are capable of estimating the total heat fluxes on the first wall due to charged particles, radiation, and charge exchange effects. To my knowledge, none can yet calculate heat fluxes on the divertor targets in fully detached conditions in a completely predictive way. In my view, we shouldn't go overboard on a simple model which only calculates one of the effects. Especially seeing as this reduced model should be used in design optimisation of the first wall shape, and not detailed analysis.

It is clear that there are pros and cons to both approaches

Ivan prefers to follow the (N, 3) approach as:
* this is used in FreeCAD which operates on `Base.Vector` and `Base.Point`
* the meshing module is also likely to use (N, 3)

* comments above regarding readability
* some modules also use (3, N)
* my take is that the implementation details (in practice simple transposing of arrays) should be carried out under the hood, such that the user (in almost all cases) only ever operates with one shape of array

The issue here is that the revolved square ring creates an annulus of wires in the planes corresponding to the top and bottom faces of the ring. Those aren't created in any particular order so when we create a face from the boundaries (wires) in those planes we can end up with a condition where we cut an outer wire out from an inner wire, so that ends up with an empty face. Essentially we need to sort the boundaries so that the outer-most one is always handled first and we cut out from that.
Or, we revolve in from 0-180 and 180-360 and do a boolean fuse. Ivan suggested that pure revolutions are bad for meshing anyway

In terms of `p_sol` -> `P_sep`, aside from the naming convention, where probably we should go with a capital P for consistency, there is a slight issue. `P_sep` is the power _crossing_ the separatrix, whereas in theory `P_SOL` would be the total power in the scrape-off layer. There is an obvious issue for both names here, though, as we're only treating the charged particles in this solver, and really the power the we assume in the charged particles is some fraction of the total power in the SOL (we can assume the rest is radiated - let's just forget about CX for a bit). Really, and this is probably a bad name, we'd have `P_SOL_particles` or something similar, because the solver is not actually treating P_sep or P_SOL... Outside of this model, we might have something else that does `P_SOL_particles = (1-f_SOL_radiation) * P_sep` which would then become the input.

I hope that makes sense. Sorry to land in the middle on this one, but the previous name was "bad" and `P_sep` is also "bad".

I guess we can do the equilibria within a PlasmaBuilder. Note that in future, this will also have a fixed boundary equilibrium step from Fabrizio's work.

I can guarantee that we will need to store the reference equilibria resulting from the equilibrium runs, and not just in file format. Querying the equilibria (extracting flux surfaces, geometry, calculating the field from the plasma etc.) is run-of-the-mill stuff in the rest of the reactor design procedure, and I'd be loathe to load the equilibria from files each time.

Also some further points for consideration:
* An `Equilibrium` (in the free boundary sense at least) is effectively a snapshot in time
* Not all equilibria will have the same geometry (the LCFS, separatrix, and O- and X-points will move subtly, or less so, depending on how the equilibria were solved)
* Not all equilibria will have the same plasma integral values (the beta_p and l_i at start and end of flat-top may be different)
* The actual plasma profiles will also differ from SOF to EOF, even if the "reference" `p'` and `FF'` flux functions may be the same.
* There is the pesky philosophical issue of the `Breakdown` (probably better called pre-magnetisation, but let's not split hairs). In this stage there is by definition no plasma, yet it is a design-driving case for the PF system.

In the past in BLUEPRINT, we stored three distinct phases in the `EquilibriumProblem` of a `Reactor`, so premag, SOF and EOF, in so-called `Snapshot` objects, where all the state information for the equilibria, coilset, constraints, and optimisers were stored. These effectively formed load cases for other build stages.

We will need to consider what to preserve and how and where. Something tells me this is beyond the intended cabilities of `Component`.

Intuitively I think I'd go with the wrapping approach. That way we always have a 'true' reference numpy array under the hood (which is 3D) and the properties you mention would return 1D / 2D / 3D views onto that array. That should also mean that we avoid a few copies and are able to keep things in synch. We can also validate that array as it comes in and in principle support receiving (N, 3) or (3, N) but always store it internally as (3, N).

Having said that, re-implementing the full ndarray interface seems like a fairly big ask. There are a bunch of gotchas around delegating off numpy calls to your own methods, see e.g. https://towardsdatascience.com/wrapping-numpys-arrays-971e015e14bb and https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.subclassing.html.

OK, those motivations are flawed, in my opinion:
* Radiation is very well defined for this model: it doesn't get treated at all. This is a reduced model where the assumption is that you're only treating charged particle power. If you want to treat radiation and charged particles in a fully consistent way, you need to write another model.
* It's totally fine if you assume for the time being that the input to this solver is P_sep, as you say it is conservative. But it absolutely does not mean that this model is treating P_sep. In a way, this model only makes sense if you assume that simplistic "global" breakdown of P_sep = P_sep_charged + P_sep_radiation. This is a standard approach in simplified models of this type.

There is nothing stopping you from feeding P_sep into this model, but I'm afraid calling the power being treated inside the model as P_sep (or P_SOL for that matter) is just misleading. It should be `P_sep_charged` or something equivalent.

The connection length calculation can fail in a couple of ways - either by not being able to calculate the separatrix position, due to no O points being found in the system for the trial coil currents, or not being able to find the separatrix intersection with the midplane (when there isn't a separatrix that intersects the midplane for a given set of coilset currents).

Interface has 5 main classes that need to be inherited from to create a file interface for a program:

### RunMode 

you can only inherit from an empty enum it seems. When inheriting as long as the run mode exists as the enum each individual class does not have to define that run mode (as there may be nothing to do)

### Task (not inherited from for a new api)
  The basic task that the three task types inherit from (setup, run, teardown)
  The run subprocess method is set up here as some tasks other than run may want to run an external program.
  All stdout/err outputs of any external code are captured here so we can control the output. I have made a 'clean' logger (no extra formatting) because external programs may do weird things with their output we do'nt want to have to deal with.
  The parent is the grouping FileProgramInterface class which allows communication between all tasks
 
### Setup

sets up any input files including writing them. Is the storage location for params which is implicitly passed when inheriting through kwargs.

### Run 

The smallest task. Essentially should only call the program. The binary name is stored here.

### Teardown

This task deals with reading back in and processing the output data. By default it does very little as this is usually quite bespoke

### FileProgramInterface

When inheriting from this I call it solver so that you can

```
import bluemira.codes.plasmod as plasmod
plasmod.Solver(...)
```
Which I thought was nice. I add all the mappings for the code in question to the params here (passed in from the child class) , force the RunMode, Setup, Run and Teardown to inherit from the classes in this file, add a few properties for ease of access and define the `run` function which runs the whole solver. You could also pass variables in on the fly to the runmode functions through run, I thought that could be useful although I havent used it in the plasmod or process interfaces.

The only class that technically needs to be defined is RunMode. The rest can be set to None (although they will warn) or just not defined in the inherited class attributes. A really minimal inherited example, it wont actually do anything (untested but the general idea)

```python

import bluemira.codes.interface as interface

class RunMode(interface.RunMode):
    RUN = 1

class Solver(interface.FileProgramInterface):
    _runmode = RunMode
   
    def __init__(
        self,
        params,
        build_config=None,
        run_dir: Optional[str] = None,
        binary: Optional[str] = "my_prog",
    ):
        super().__init__(
            "MYPROG",
            params,
            build_config.get("mode", "run"),
            binary=binary,
            run_dir=run_dir,
            mappings=[],
            problem_settings=build_config.get("problem_settings", None),
        )

Hi @DanShort12,
thanks for raising this issue. Regarding the points that you highlighted:

- I agree on the fact that a review of the code should be made taking into account the inter-dependency of the different classes. Considering the state of the art of bluemira, this is a good moment since the code is still "manageable" and a reorganization of some classes/modules would not take too much effort (and should not drastically change the user interface). However, a refactor is unuseful if we don't have a clear idea of which classes/modules are the "roots" of our infrastructure and build the rest (with an "including" strategy) on top of that (not "inside" them). As a starting point, we could review the display module that, considering the old implementation and the new WIP one, PR #527, is a perfect example of how there could be two different visions of inter-dependency and integration of the same code in different classes.
- I am in favor of using `TYPE_CHECKING` or, alternatively, `from __future__ import annotations`(that should do the same). I am the first one that didn't use it and it would have been solved different problems in the past ^_^'
- Regarding the use of `__init__.py`, it seems to me that there isn't really a consensus on what is the best practice, so nothing contrary in letting it empty and importing any function/class with its full "path". However, we should also have an eye on the evolution of our code and on the user interface. One of the `__init__.py` applications is to import key functions from various modules directly into the package namespace. In this way, one can restructure the internal modules without messing up with the API for the end-users (practically defined by the imports in the `__init__.py` file). I think we should consider also this strategy (at least for some modules). In any case, IMHO, this point is strongly connected to the first one. A good hierarchic architecture should not bring to all that problems when importing something in `__init__.py`.
@DanShort12 @je-cook yeah, a script to install PLASMOD into the codes directory is necessary. But perhaps that can come once we're actually using the PLASMOD repo (or a branch on there somewhere).
Hi @jmorris-uk - if you're happy with the wording here then can we get this in?

I agree that, ideally, importing things from the module `__init__.py` rather than the full path should be what users do, and that we should facilitate that. This ideal situation is apparently much harder to deliver from the outset, though, so I think we should prioritise usability, rather than ease of importing. Many examples break because of circular imports, and many pipelines have failed because of circular imports.

I think that relative imports inside modules have caused more havoc that anything else, and the user shouldn't care how internal imports are handled. We can just use full path imports inside modules to sidestep issues related to circular imports, and it would also allow the files inside modules to be run as scripts, which is a serious benefit when developing / debugging (for some, depending on how you develop / debug).

We've seen that moving the plotting and display away from the things that we are plotting / displaying has introduced a whole host of circular import issues. I honestly don't care about the "architecture" per se, I care about being able to plot things easily, and not having circular import issues. It does make sense to me that thing that handles the plotting for an object `X` lives in the same module as object `X`. I think this would be easier to maintain.

So my two cents:
* get rid of imports in `__init__.py` for now
* get rid of relative imports inside modules
* reshuffle some stuff to address some circular import issues
* do not shy away from doing delayed imports in certain modules / functions whatever
* once everything settles down, put the main user-facing classes and functions inside `__init__.py` of each module

Hi @je-cook, thanks for the clarification. I am going to close this issue and just open a request for the creation of a mock example with plasmod.
I think we can consider this closed

Fundamentally, all we are displaying in the `display` module at the moment is geometry. We're certainly not going to be displaying any CAD that does not come from geometry.

In terms of plotting, we could in future display contours for 2-D scalar fields and the like, and other general results, but at the risk of ending up wrapping matplotlib and of endlessly trying to standardise different plots (where sometimes one approach looks better than the other) is high, in my opinion. I'm also wondering (after the fact) why `geometry` and `display` are even different modules. Note that a whole bunch of other modules (e.g. equilibria, magnetostatics, balance of plant) handle their plotting internally to the module. Philosophically we went for being able to "replace" any module with another one, and the corollary, that any module be as standalone as possible. Personally, I consider display and plotting to be a fundamental part of what each module does. From this standpoint, I no longer see why `display` is separate from `geometry`, seeing as the former exclusively serves the latter.

I'm leaning towards having a set of tools (perhaps above and beyond what we already have) in `find.py` and `physics.py`. Admittedly these could be better documented and their existence better displayed to the user.

My problem with having an EquilibriumAnalyser class is that it will have many and diverse responsibilities:
* geometry extraction (LCFS, separatrix, O-+X-points, OMP, etc.)
* flux surface quantity calculations (kappa, delta, q, etc.)
* plasma integral parameter calculations (beta_p, l_i, etc.)
* plasma profile extraction (jtor, pressure, q, etc.)

These could all live on one class, but I think it would probably end up being a namespace with one shared attribute (the equilibrium), as most of these methods wouldn't talk to each other at all.

I think that some methods on `Equilibrium` could be split out into these tools, though I do think that a couple of commonly used ones (find_OX_points, or get_LCFS or get_separatrix) should probably stay as they are so common.

Thoughts, @alexanderianblair ?

Perhaps a good example to follow: https://github.com/boutproject/BOUT-dev/blob/master/CITATION.cff

The decision there seems to be to list all the contributors and point to a single paper. Seeing as we will have publications on BLUEMIRA in future, we can add that paper later. For now, if we have to pick one, I would pick none, and just point the users to the README, where the relevant publications are already listed.

The above is on an EU-DEMO 2015 equilibrium with CREATE's calculation assumed to be correct. Couple of simple corrections on axis and at separatrix required for the "new" approach.

The safety factor calculation in `ClosedFluxSurface` whilst fancier and an attempt at a more physical approach was just plain old wrong, it seems. I didn't plot it here as I'm a little ashamed of not having checked it in the first place. Suffice to say it's bad.

Some rather painstaking stuff delivers the "new" calc in the plot above, which seems to be marginally more accurate than the old approximation (apparently remarkably good - for conventional A equilibria, at least) approach. I'll keep digging to see if I can find a balance between speed and accuracy at a range of grid discretisations and aspect ratios (or rather ST vs conventional) because this would constitute a better benchmark.

Much nicer layout!

> Much nicer implementation for 3D now, and good to see that the xz casing is now available. I can see we're starting to get a few functions that e.g. populate xz from the 3D design, which is probably ok for now, but we might eventually want to think about isolating those - at the moment if we wanted to 2D design then we'd need to make a 3D design first... perhaps that's a logical constraint on the design, but it could start to make things feel a bit spaghetti-like.

Agreed, I'm not very happy with having to build 3-D in order to get 2-D. A very real immediate problem will be constraining the inner casing shape w.r.t the keep-out zone with the optimisation of the TF current centreline. So for every iteration we'd need to do a whole bunch of 3-D Boolean operations etc. just to get back to a 2-D x-z.

Problem is that to do a variable thickness offset we can only resort to some operations on coordinates (not primitives) and then fit a spline to those. In order to do this robustly we'd need to be able to fit a spline whilst setting the start and end tangencies (see #516). Otherwise we're going to see some pretty weird splines for sure.

I think it may be better for simplicity to add all of those things in a new PR.

I think a refactor of `inscribed_rect` is needed, and probably both interpolators should have access to it. That would make the flow the same. For a path that would then give you a strip. It wouldn't matter that the strip could be concave because the old `inscribed_rect` already deals with that (its only the optimiser that has that issue).

The tools to breakdown the PF track into interpolator paths feels the same as creating a region for the RegionInterpolator. It would be good if the function could be easily generic (even if only the track is implemented for now).

From that I see CS coils as a special case of PathInterpolator with one coordinate. You could even just call PathInterpolator with straight tracks. The tracks will already be split by the time they get to the PositionMapper anyway.

I just didn't want to assume that it would be generic enough. Arguably, the whole approach of doing the coil position interpolation this way is just "one way of doing it", and the creation of individual segments for individual coils is equally questionable. section-properties <v2 limits our scipy version to < 1.6. But v2 and newer require a matplotlib >3.3.4 which we are limited at the moment from #234

I've applied these updates locally, but had to run this to get `llvmlite` to upgrade:

pip install -r requirements.txt --ignore-installed llvmlite

```

Just running through the full test suite locally after that in case it introduces any issues.

Fine with me after a local run of the tests. Probably worth asking users to try upgrading normally with `conda env update -f conda/environment.yml --prune` and then to do `pip install -r requirements.txt --ignore-installed llvmlite` if needed.

As we have just updated to occt 7.5.1 (because of the freecad dependency in #556) pythonocc needs to be upgraded. Locally testing this the test fails. It looks like there is a bug in pythonocc:
```python
shp_label.AddAttribute(TDataStd_Name(), True)
*** TypeError: in method 'TDF_Label_AddAttribute', argument 2 of type 'opencascade::handle< TDF_Attribute > const &'
```
This is odd because `TDataStd_Name` inherits from `TDF_Attribute` see the [docs](https://dev.opencascade.org/doc/occt-7.5.0/refman/html/class_t_data_std___name.html). Also on pythonocc 7.4.1:

```python
ipdb> isinstance(occ_name, TDF_Attribute)
True
```
Whereas on pythonocc 7.5.1
```python
ipdb> isinstance(occ_name, TDF_Attribute)
False
```

Just as a note on this, a generator will raise an `StopIteration` error whenever it reaches the end of the iterable - even if that iterable has effectively zero length. As an example the following will execute the same values as many times as you want (always returning 6):

```python
next(filter(lambda val: val > 5, [4, 5, 6]))
```

While the following will always error because it's trying to get the next value of a generator formed from an empty iterable:

```python
next(filter(lambda val: val > 5, [1, 2, 3]))
```

Looking at the original error here, I suspect the second run of `make_2d_profile` was encountering a scenario where there were no points outward of whatever value was assigned to `x_compare` at the time. I see this has been fixed by removing the second call, but figured worth noting in case anyone comes back to this to look at fixing the root cause (either not using a generator in that function, or handling the `StopIteration` error in the function that calls it). @sebkahn @je-cook

P.S. I think you can actually see this condition in the print out above:

- The first call has the following, so presumably the `find_outer_point` logic gets the second `plane_ints` element:

```python
compare_x = 2.5311508616605125
plane_ints = [[2.13115086, 0. -6.98318023], [ 3.03115086, 0., -6.98318023]]
```

- The second call has the following, so there are no longer any `plane_int` values with a first element that is larger than `compare_x`, which will raise a `StopIteration` error when the next value is extracted from the generator:

```python
compare_x = 2.5311508616605125
plane_ints = [[2.13114981, 0., -6.98318023]]
```

1. We seem to be keeping to separation of concerns fairly well, and I like how the logic for making the geometry is separated out from the solving of optimisation problems / reading previous result / mocking. It could be useful to break some of the build functions down further so that there are individual functions for each component.

2. The callable logic on builders can be a bit fiddly, and as seen in #589 this can lead to some complications when arguments need to be passed to one method but not another. It may be worth unwinding this and just having the user make separate calls to the relevant methods (at least until there are enough examples to factor the problem back down into a form that works in all cases).

3. Related to 2., we're currently doing quite a bit that hides the real signatures of the builder methods. This leads to too much use of `**kwargs` and results in it being unclear how a method should be called because e.g. the IDE doesn't know what arguments can be passed in, or what help text is available. I think this is one of the main issues at the moment, and probably warrants some of this being unwound.

4. The run/read/mock can be a bit tricky to use when arguments need to be passed into the design problem. This leads tothe different modes needing to be called differently, which then ends up hiding what's needed for the actual method from the user (as for 3. this is seen in a resulting proliferation of `**kwargs` to cope with this).

I think my main gripe from the points I've listed so far is that we're doing quite a bit to hide functionality from the user, which results in the usage being obscured or at least hard to discover e.g. in an IDE.

It would certainly be possible to write some logic into `show_cad` to view sectors and so on, or to have a broader view selector. I was thinking though that a build following the same steps as the full one would be more representative than effectively adding in additional build steps (cutting and so on) in the display. I was also thinking this way is more extensible, since other use cases can satisfy whatever view they want via their builder, rather than having to also write their own displayer.

I think the alternative models would be supported today by adding in alternative build methods (on top of `build_xz` etc.) - of course there may need to be some refactoring along with that when the need arises.

> Works well for me +1 . I noticed that, for the case I'm testing, the legs don't extend all the way to the x-point. Is this OK/to be expected? > > Yeah so this is due to the way we get the separatrix at present, with the old approach in `StreamFlow` doing a bunch of cute stuff under the hood to upsample things, without direct knowledge of the field. With this way we start from the more or less "true" position of the X-point, which due to interpolation the separatrix does not pass through at the moment. Because we use some interpolation on psi and that means that any turning points occur on a grid point, which the X-point is almost never on. It's a known issue with `find_LCFS_separatrix` that the extrema are not totally correctly captured.

I used the collection of the tests into a class to handle controlling the regeneration of the json files, but can break that out into separate actions. I'll redo this so that it's easier to see how things move around.

Good suggestion on breaking out the invocation though.

@CoronelBuendia, @je-cook, @DanShort12, not sure if it is a good approach to suggest a user (or a developer) import BluemiraWire from face.py (just to refer to the example reported in the description of this PR).
My preferred solution would instead be to use the __init__.py of each module to create the conventional public API exposed by the module. In this specific case, I would prefer to add in geometry/__init__.py all the necessary imports:
```
from .bound_box import BoundingBox
from .coordinates import Coordinates
from .wire import BluemiraWire
from .face import BluemiraFace
from .shell import BluemiraShell
from .plane import BluemiraPlane
...
```
and then, when it is necessary, do the import as:
1) for internal files
```
from . import BluemiraWire
```
2) for external files
```
import bluemira.geometry as geo
bmwire = geo.BluemiraWire(.....)
```
I know that the suggest approach could bring to the usual cyclic import problems, but probably we can solve with the TYPE_CHECKING.

Another alternative solution, if the problem is just for geometry, would be to join all the files related to geometries (i.e. wires.py, face.py, etc.) into the base.py (so, all in a file, like we have for the Components).

What are your thoughts?

The only thing that matters for me is that the user can import things from a certain module without needing to know exactly where such a thing might live inside the module.

So, I also think that certain key classes and functions should be imported inside `__init__.py` such that they are accessible at the module level.

We are however a long way off sorting out these circular import issues, and until such a time as we can actually expose everything at the module level, all this PR is doing is protecting the namespaces from `from somewhere import *`. We'd probably keep these `__all__` fields even with importing everything at the module level. Pretty sure most modern IDEs will pick them up when you change the name of a class or function, too.

I was hoping that defining __all__ would also stop IDEs from showing that you can import `BluemiraGeo` from e.g. `bluemira.geometry.face`, but sadly my VS Code doesn't seem to check all before showing me the options of what I can import from a file. Perhaps I have my settings wrong..

I think that relative imports inside modules are unnecessary and we actually had to get rid of them in the past because they were causing a lot of pain when we were moving things around. In practice, from the user perspective, it makes no difference if we use full path imports or relative imports. One is more explicit and the other less so. With modern IDEs I honestly don't see the disadvantage of full path imports. The user certainly will not care; it's about what is easier for us to manage, and we have been burnt trying to use relative imports everywhere.

I don't have any strong opinions on `from somewhere import something as sw` + `sw.Something(...)` or `from somewhere import Something` + `Something(...)`

Hello

This issue should address the STEP reactor design issue forcing us to re-create `Coils` and `Coilsets` instead of updating them. The position not being propagated to the 2D shapes.

@CoronelBuendia suggested it was related to the coil corners not being updated and @alexanderianblair suggested another issue for the coil meshing.

Question: why storing the corners? Could we calculated them only when we want to output them? Having the coil position and its size should be enough to define its geometry, no?

The solution propose by everyone is do define accessors for both `Coil` and `SymmetricCircuits`, setters and getters that ensure all the coil consistuent are updated consistently.

A good test for this issue PR is to have STEP reactor design having its `Coil`s updated instead of re-created when modified and still having a working setup.

I think this goes back to whether the `systems_code_solver` function (and other similar possible functions) become a class themselves. I'm mildly against that in its current form.

Possibly the solver object should have plotters associated with it but it feels odd to me because it is not, in my head at least, part of the solver itself. 
It seems to me that it is post processing on the solver output which should be a separate thing.

Maybe what we need is some solver post processing mechanics. It might be hard to build that with only one method to build from

Just cleaning up, but I think this is nearly ready. A quick summary for those who may not have been roped in on everything.

It is not correct for a free boundary equilibrium solution to exactly recreate the profiles of a fixed boundary solution, whilst also prescribing plasma current. You can either:
* take the profiles from somewhere, not prescribe Ip, get to keep those profiles exactly, but not get the same current as a fixed boundary solver would. This is because the plasma volume is inherently different once X-points are accounted for, which many fixed boundary solvers do not treat.
* take the profiles from somewhere, prescribe Ip, get those profiles scaled accordingly to match the desired plasma current.

This is the state of affairs for the latter option, on the private ST test we have (I believe it is SPR-08):
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/26097289/154642050-1acea18a-fc05-4eb8-8407-dba4f16b24a2.png)

Here for example you can see that the BLUEMIRA toroidal current density profile is lower (in absolute terms) than the JETTO one. That's because the volume is slightly larger (X-points) such that the current density can be lower across the profile to recover the same plasma current.

Note that I have flipped the signs of the flux functions here to get this plot to look good. We need to more generally treat the signs of Ip, Bt, and flux functions in the coordinate convention issue: #318

f, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.contourf(xx, zz, B[1])
ax.plot(p.x, p.z)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
```

@CoronelBuendia, I would propose the following steps to close this issue:

1. create a `transport_solver` class that interfaces with PLASMOD (or, in future, other transport codes) and provides `p'` and `FF'`
2. create a 2D fem-fixed-boundary GS solver that calculates `J_plasma` for given  `p'` and `FF'` coming from a `transport_solver` object
3. create an equilibrium class that iterates between PLASMOD and GS ensuring convergence on specific parameters

As support of step2, a 2D-fem magnetostatic solver is necessary.

A single issue can be created for each of these steps (as already discussed).

A few code style and misc comments. I've given this a bit of poking:

(NOTE: TaperedPictureFrame fails with lack of tangency, @shaildesai96  is this expected?)

```python
from bluemira.geometry.tools import sweep_shape, make_polygon
from bluemira.geometry.parameterisations import PictureFrame, TaperedPictureFrame, FullDomeFlatInnerCurvedPictureFrame, BotDomeFlatInnerCurvedPictureFrame, TopDomeFlatInnerCurvedPictureFrame
from copy import deepcopy
import numpy as np
from bluemira.display import show_cad

dr, dy = 0.2, 0.4
xs = make_polygon({"x":[-dr, dr, dr, -dr], "y":[-dy, -dy, dy, dy], "z":0}, closed=True)

shapes  = []
results = []
offset = 0
for p in [PictureFrame, TaperedPictureFrame, FullDomeFlatInnerCurvedPictureFrame, BotDomeFlatInnerCurvedPictureFrame, TopDomeFlatInnerCurvedPictureFrame]:
    cross_section = deepcopy(xs)
    shape = p().create_shape()
    shapes.append(shape)
    x_min = np.min(shape.discretize(ndiscr=100, byedges=True).x)
    cross_section.translate((x_min, 0, 0))
    try:
        result = sweep_shape(cross_section, shape)
        result.translate((0, offset, 0))
        results.append(result)
    except:
        print(p.__name__)
        pass
    offset += 3
```

> The decorator is a good addition.
> 
> Not 100% sure how I feel about the `stage` argument being extracted into a class member instead of being passed into the `_build_stage`, etc., functions. If/when I forget to decorate my design stage, I'm probably going to be confused about why one of my stages is building twice (because `self.stage` hasn't been updated). In my opinion, using a function argument is more explicit. State is generally more difficult to keep track of (and debug) than locally scoped variables, at least for me. Let me know what you think, completely up to you.

I considered not using `self.stage` as I agree it could lead to exactly the situation you describe, possibly deleting the attribute after a stage (within the decorator) could be the way forward and then modifying `__getattribute__` to catch a missing stage and return a understandable error. I wanted to reduce the amount a new developer had to remember, but this could be too far

Issue update after meeting discussion.

## Description of issue / requirement to address
This feature should be initially only implemented in the Power Cycle. Later analysis can establish whether it should be implemented in a more higher-level class, accessible from every module.

## Proposed solution
Implement a dedicated JSON input file, exclusive to the Power Cycle module, that establishes preferences in terms of units for tables, diagrams and plots. Apply unit conversion in each particular data-visualization method, based on these inputs.

I've narrowed this down to the two different constructors we have for circle arcs; `make_circle` and `make_circle_arc_3P`.

The problem is that when you use `make_circle_arc_3P`, the underlying Curve has a Rotation, which is not transferable to the reconstruction function `make_circle`.

```python
from bluemira.codes._freecadapi import make_circle, make_circle_arc_3P

ca_3P = make_circle_arc_3P([1, 0, 2], [2, 0, 3], [0, 0, 3.2])
ca_3P_e = ca_3P.Edges[0]
ca_3P_c = ca_3P_e.Curve

print("Original circle arc by 3 points")
print(ca_3P_e.FirstParameter)
print(ca_3P_e.LastParameter)

print(ca_3P_c.Radius)
print(ca_3P_c.Center)
print(ca_3P_c.Axis)

ca_r = make_circle(ca_3P_c.Radius, ca_3P_c.Center, ca_3P_e.FirstParameter, ca_3P_e.LastParameter, axis=ca_3P_c.Axis)
ca_r_e = ca_r.Edges[0]
ca_r_c = ca_r_e.Curve

print("Reconstructed circle arc")
print(ca_r_e.FirstParameter)
print(ca_r_e.LastParameter)

print(ca_r_c.Radius)
print(ca_r_c.Center)
print(ca_r_c.Axis)


print(ca_3P_c.Rotation)
print(ca_r_c.Rotation)
```

Hi Charles,

That does sound odd.. I've never seen that before, and nothing similar on native Ubuntu. We've had pivy/coin issues in the past though.

I take it you've installed recently, which means it's less likely to be a dependency problem... it does not however rule it out. @je-cook could you take a look into this?

> If the tests pass... then fine by me. That said, just because one can do just about anything in Python, doesn't mean that we should! This quite complex packaging for quite simple behaviour feels slightly unnerving. I worry that it will be brittle and difficult to understand / modify. I'm happy with it if it works and we can move forwards, but it scares me!

I would say that it is the same as a function that creates and modifies an instance of the class and calls it (thereby the function being the outward facing UX). I preferred this way as to the user they still create a class instance for all the parameterisations. I think there is probably still some room for improvement but I can't see it right now. 

I see complex shaped pictureframes as a mostly advanced feature either way and I think we need to be very careful adding more to it in future. At least now it is easier to read the build function and if we could consolidate those inputs to be the same it may be a good future improvement.

Hi, this seems very closely related to #997. I've seen I think the same error while working to fix that. I'll update here when I have some news.

I think your install is fine Charles, this is on our end, for now 2D viewing should still work and you can save individual shapes with the `geometry.tools.save_as_STEP` function and open the resulting CAD file in your favourite CAD program (eg freecad). Fixing this seems easy, but testing it is not so simple. I can add a test like the following to `TestParameterFrame`. This passes when only `TestParameterFrame` is run, but fails when it's run as part of the test suite.

```python
class TestParameterFrame:

    def test_init_with_defaults_sets_no_parameters(self):
        pf = ParameterFrame(with_defaults=True)

        # Defaults are empty on base class; expect nothing to be set
        assert len(pf.get_parameter_list()) == 0
```

This is down to the class method `ParameterFrame.set_default_params`, which edits the `ParameterFrame` definition with some default parameters. The method is called in the class definition of `Configuration`. So, if the above test is run _before_ `Configuration` is imported somewhere, it passes. If it's run _after_ `Configuration` is imported, the test fails (this is easy to confirm by importing `Configuration` at the start of the test).

I think this could cause some subtle bugs down-the-line. Perhaps this issue can wait until we've had our discussions on `ParameterFrame`'s design.

We talked in the past about removing the default mechanics from ParameterFrame and I think we ended on removing after we had removed BLUEPRINT and set up the new reactor build. Then we can move all the 'default' values out to some file.

Updated to latest Ubuntu.

Ubuntu 22.04 no longer packages sub versions of python so this is built on the default python (3.10), there are some hacks at the end because of this that need to be done with a couple of packages that aren't updated for 3.10 yet.

I've also patched the qt5 build in the same way that kde have because of a gcc compilation problem. Possilbe other solution is to pull from their repo.

The `--limited-api=yes` is not a great addition to the pyside install either but it builds and I've had no issues since.

Main remaining issue other than that is getting pivy to install properly, it builds but crashes when I try to run any CAD viewer (same as #1020), pivy==0.6.5 (#1048) has some run issues about circular importing. If I pull across the #1033 I can view things however so it feels like the last hurdle.

As far as I'm aware all other dependencies are now included (apart from neutroincs material maker which we probably should upgrade), I havent run pytest yet though, just the EUDEMO example.
This should stay WIP until the hacks bash script can be removed.

- There's also some discussion to be had on what stance we take on bugfixes on old releases.

Good things to think about, here's my initial thoughts

> I'm assuming semantic.

I think semantic makes more sense than calendar based probably but not wedded to that.

> Do we stick with 0.0.1aX and increment X for the time being?

Yeah I think so. Once we have something we're happy with go straight to 0.1.0 and then point release every 6 weeks makes the most sense to me. We can always go back to alphas if we need to.

> Will we backport bugfixes...?

I think bugfix backport releases probably shouldnt be needed until at least 0.2 (or maybe 1.0 onwards) at a minimum before that we should insist on the latest version being used.
